clinicalPearls: Fibroids are benign monoclonal smooth-muscle tumours and the commonest pelvic tumour of reproductive-age women; the majority are asymptomatic and discovered incidentally.
Growth is oestrogen- and progesterone-dependent, so lesions tend to enlarge during pregnancy and typically regress after the menopause.
The FIGO leiomyoma classification (types 0 to 8) localises lesions from submucosal through intramural to subserosal; submucosal fibroids most affect menstrual bleeding and fertility.
Heavy menstrual bleeding is the dominant symptom and may lead to iron-deficiency anaemia, whereas subserosal and pedunculated lesions rarely cause bleeding.
Bulk-related symptoms such as pelvic pressure, urinary frequency and constipation reflect large or subserosal lesions rather than the bleeding pattern.
Red (carneous) degeneration classically causes acute pain in mid-pregnancy; other degenerative changes include hyaline, cystic and calcific.
Rapid enlargement, or any growth after the menopause, should raise concern for leiomyosarcoma even though malignant transformation is very rare.

Management is individualised across expectant, medical (antifibrinolytics, hormonal therapy, gonadotrophin-releasing hormone analogues, selective progesterone receptor modulators), uterine artery embolisation and surgery (myomectomy or hysterectomy), guided by symptoms and fertility wishes.
reference.pathophysiology: A fibroid arises from a single transformed myometrial smooth-muscle cell that proliferates as a monoclonal nodule of smooth muscle within an abundant extracellular matrix of collagen, fibronectin and proteoglycan, giving the characteristic whorled cut surface and a surrounding pseudocapsule of compressed myometrium. Growth is driven by oestrogen and progesterone, with overexpression of their receptors and of local growth factors, and somatic MED12 mutations are frequently implicated. Heavy menstrual bleeding results from distortion and enlargement of the endometrial surface, dysregulation of vasoactive and angiogenic factors, and impaired local haemostasis, while enlarging lesions produce pressure effects on adjacent pelvic viscera.
additionalDifferentials: Intrauterine pregnancy causing an enlarged uterus
additionalInvestigations: Full blood count to assess for anaemia
Transvaginal with or without transabdominal ultrasound as first-line imaging
Saline infusion sonohysterography to delineate submucosal lesions
Diagnostic and operative hysteroscopy for submucosal fibroids
Pelvic MRI for mapping, distinguishing adenomyosis and planning embolisation or surgery
Endometrial biopsy when abnormal bleeding is accompanied by risk factors for hyperplasia
redFlags: Rapidly enlarging mass, or any growth after the menopause, suggesting leiomyosarcoma
Severe symptomatic anaemia from heavy bleeding, potentially requiring transfusion
Acute severe pelvic pain from torsion of a pedunculated fibroid or red degeneration
Urinary retention or hydronephrosis from mass effect
Postmenopausal bleeding requiring exclusion of endometrial pathology
reference.prognosis: The prognosis is excellent as fibroids are benign, with most remaining asymptomatic and stable and symptomatic lesions responding well to treatment and regressing after the menopause. Recurrence can follow myomectomy, and malignant transformation is exceptionally rare.
pitfalls: Attributing all abnormal uterine bleeding to fibroids and missing coexistent endometrial hyperplasia or carcinoma.
Failing to consider leiomyosarcoma before morcellation, particularly in postmenopausal or rapidly growing masses.
Overlooking coexisting adenomyosis, which frequently mimics and accompanies fibroids.
Neglecting to correct iron-deficiency anaemia before intervention.
Assuming subserosal or pedunculated fibroids are the cause of heavy menstrual bleeding.
